title: Ulyana and the Will
premise: True-crime podcaster Lior Brightwater receives two letters about the thirty-year-old Brightwater estate fire that killed their parents: one confessing to arson, the other promising 'the rest of the truth' if Lior keeps digging. As Lior reopens the case, they discover their beloved found family—the aunt who raised them and the family lawyer who managed the will—wove alibis to protect someone they loved. The trail leads to a hidden second will and a half-sibling no one acknowledged, forcing Lior to choose between exposing the truth and preserving the only family they have left. In the end, Lior broadcasts the full story, justice arrives outside a courtroom, and the found family, fractured by honesty, slowly rebuilds on firmer ground.
about_author: Coral Oyelaran is a former paralegal who spent a decade reading wills, probate filings, and the quiet lies families tell each other before turning those observations into fiction. She writes mysteries about inheritance, memory, and the people who keep secrets out of love.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Handwriting
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. On the eve of closing their podcast's final season, Lior receives twin letters about the Brightwater fire: a confession signed with their mother's name, and an unsigned note promising more if they dig. The emotional beat is dread disguised as excitement—Lior has built a career on other people's cold cases precisely to avoid their own.

chapters.title: The Aunt Who Never Locked Doors
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Returning to the decaying Brightwater house, Lior interviews Aunt Marguerite, whose warm evasions don't match her famously open-door habits. A locked attic room and a missing box of legal papers raise the first real question. The beat is unease: home feels staged, like a set dressed for an audience of one.

chapters.title: Alibi in Triplicate
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, with podcast transcript interludes. Pulling trial records, Lior finds three witnesses—Aunt Marguerite, lawyer Desmond Hale, and groundskeeper Tomas—whose statements align too perfectly for people who claim they barely spoke that night. The beat is the thrill of the hunt curdling as Lior realizes the conspiracy may include everyone who raised them.

chapters.title: What the Fire Didn't Take
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV, thirty years ago. A flashback chapter: Tomas saw someone leave the east wing that night and was paid—gently, kindly—to forget. His loyalty was to a grieving child, not a lie. The beat is tragic tenderness, showing how protection and deception became indistinguishable.

chapters.title: The Second Will
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Following probate irregularities, Lior finds evidence of a later will that disinherited them entirely—and names an unknown beneficiary. Confronting Desmond Hale, they get a lawyer's non-answers delivered with genuine affection. The beat is betrayal sharpening into resolve; Lior stops asking whether to dig and starts asking how deep.

chapters.title: A Sister Made of Paperwork
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The trail leads to Vera, a hospice nurse living under another name—Lior's half-sibling, the unacknowledged daughter written out before the fire. Vera denies everything but knows details only an insider could. The beat is vertigo: the stranger across the table shares Lior's eyes and possibly their motive.

chapters.title: Confession, Revised
chapters.summary: Alternating Lior and Vera POVs. A second letter arrives—a corrected confession admitting the first was forged to draw Lior home. Someone wanted this reopened, but who? Marguerite collapses under questioning, and Lior realizes the letters were bait aimed at the family, not at them. The beat is fear: Lior isn't the investigator anymore; they're the weapon.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, present day. Cornered, Marguerite finally tells the truth: she covered for her dying sister—Lior's mother—who started the fire accidentally during a confrontation over the new will, and died believing she'd killed no one. The alibis were mercy. The beat is devastating compassion; every lie was an act of love.

chapters.title: The Trial That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. With the statute long expired, Lior faces a choice: broadcast the truth or bury it. Instead they gather everyone—Vera, Tomas, Hale, Marguerite—in the burned wing and let each tell their piece aloud, no edits, no episode. The beat is catharsis through exposure; truth spoken together hurts less than truth leaked apart.

chapters.title: Brightwater, After
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, epilogue frame. The final podcast episode airs—not the confession, but the story of a family that lied itself into being and chose to stop. Vera stays; Marguerite unlocks the attic door for good; the anonymous letter-writer is revealed as Hale, who wanted the weight lifted before he died. The beat is quiet, earned peace: justice outside the law, family rebuilt on truth.
